Background terms (plain nodes) form dense\n  communities joined by a few inter-community edges. Pool concepts (bold black rings) sit on the periphery\n  of communities, mostly in the gaps between two of them, where they act as bridge or connector nodes; three\n  are labelled as examples (\\emph{wireless backhaul}, \\emph{EPR steering}, \\emph{holographic QCD}). The full\n  network comprises approximately 27,000 nodes and 84,000 edges; the panel is an illustrative rendering of\n  its high-degree core for readability.}\n  \\label{fig:network}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\subsection{Structural precursors of emergence}\n\\label{sec:rq1method}\n\n\\paragraph{Emergence labels.} We defined sustained uptake as a concept-year reaching at least 20 papers per\nyear and gaining at least 20 percentile points in co-word network strength relative to the focal population.\nThe focal-population label was declared before outcomes were computed.\n\n\\paragraph{Matched event study.} For each concept showing sustained uptake, we matched it to a control concept\nfrom the same first-appearance band and origin field that did not show sustained uptake, using 1:1\nnearest-neighbour matching on pre-period network indicators. The standardised mean difference (Cohen's $S$)\nbetween treated and control concepts at lags $k = -3$ to $0$ is the estimand. Bootstrap confidence intervals\n($B = 2{,}000$) and Holm-corrected $p$-values control for multiple testing. The Screen fold (202 concepts)\nproduced 68 onsets and 26 matched pairs.\n\n\\paragraph{Openness measures.} To test whether pre-emergence closure is reducible to neighbourhood turnover\nor Burt brokerage, we computed four variants: (a) turnover-residualised closure, obtained by regressing\nclosure on the new-relation rate, novelty, Baselga beta-similarity, log volume, concept age and Shannon\nentropy; (b) persistent-neighbour closure, restricting the closure coefficient to the top-20 neighbours\npresent in both year $y$ and $y{-}1$; (c) Burt constraint and effective size of the weighted ego\nnetwork~\\citep{Burt2004}; and (d) cross-community pair excess, defined as the count of partner pairs from\ndistinct Leiden communities minus the count expected under a strength-decile null.\n\n\\subsection{Host-entry grafting}\n\\label{sec:rq2method}\n\n\\paragraph{Host-entry events.} A host-entry event is the first year in which a concept appears in a\nnon-origin subfield together with at least five co-occurring partner terms. From 4,177 main-arm host entries,\nthe Screen fold retains 1,544 events across 140 concept clusters after the partner-count filter.\n\n\\paragraph{Exposure variable.} Host-vocabulary share (denoted $A_\\text{cont}$ in tables) is the tag-weighted\nmean of each partner's pre-entry publication share in the host subfield, where tag-weighted means that each\nco-occurrence edge is weighted by its association strength. The continuous measure is primary because only\n1.1\\% of partner tags have a host share above 50\\%. Co-transfer (denoted CT in tables) is the fraction of\npartners that were origin companions of the concept in the five years before entry.\n\n\\paragraph{Outcome.} Five-year newcomer uptake: the count of host-subfield papers by author-disjoint newcomers\n(authors with no prior concept paper and no co-authorship with concept authors) during the five years after entry.\n\n\\paragraph{Model.} Poisson pseudo-maximum-likelihood (PPML) regression~\\citep{Silva2006} with\nconcept-clustered standard errors~\\citep{Cameron2015}. Two specifications were pre-registered. The primary\nspecification includes concept-by-entry-year and host-by-entry-year fixed effects. The co-primary specification\nincludes concept, entry-year and host fixed effects and was declared for use when the primary drops below 30\nconcept clusters (which it does on the Held-out fold). Both specifications include co-transfer as a second\nregressor.\n\n\\paragraph{Held-out fold.} 93 concepts, 1,100 entries; minimum detectable effect (co-primary): IRR per\nstandard deviation of 1.15. The fold was used during pipeline development (event counts, population sizes and\ngating decisions were computed on both folds), so its grafting estimate is a development-set estimate, not a\ntrue held-out confirmation.\n\n\\paragraph{MeSH replication.} The same analysis was applied to 191 MeSH concepts. Because the pre-declared\npartner-count rule yielded only 192 events, the pre-declared relaxation was triggered, producing 2,171 events\nacross 160 concept clusters.\n\n\\subsection{Post-confirmation decomposition}\n\\label{sec:decomposition}\n\nAfter the Held-out and MeSH tests confirmed the host-vocabulary effect, three exploratory decompositions were\npre-specified and frozen before any coefficient was read:\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n\\item \\textbf{Extensive versus intensive margins.} A linear probability model for whether any newcomer uptake\noccurs (extensive margin), and PPML conditional on uptake having started (intensive margin). Inverse-variance\nweighting (IVW) pools estimates across the Screen, Held-out and MeSH folds.\n\n\\item \\textbf{Host-specific versus generic accessibility.} Generality proxies (tag-weighted normalised subfield\nentropy and log block frequency of each partner) are added as controls. The Balassa-index lift\nmeasure~\\citep{Balassa1965}, defined as the log ratio of the host-vocabulary share to the partner's baseline\nsubfield share, is tested as an alternative exposure variable.\n\n\\item \\textbf{Origin-field dependence.} A Wald test of equality across origin-field groups (Physics and\nAstronomy, Computer Science, other).\n\\end{itemize}\n\n\\section{Results}\n\\label{sec:results}\n\n\\subsection{Structural precursors of emergence}\n\\label{sec:rq1results}\n\n\\subsubsection{Closure measures}\n\nOn the Screen fold, concepts that later show sustained uptake have lower general closure in the years before\nonset (matched event study $S = -0.44$, 95\\% CI $-0.81$ to $-0.05$; pooled panel $S = -0.74$, 95\\% CI $-1.06$\nto $-0.46$). The pre-registered positive sign was not observed; the effect runs in the opposite direction.\n\n\\begin{table}[!htbp]\n\\centering\n\\caption{Closure on the Held-out fold (development-set estimate).}\n\\label{tab:closure}\n\\footnotesize\n\\begin{tabularx}{\\linewidth}{X c c c c l}\n\\toprule\nMeasure & Screen $S$ & HO $S$ & HO 95\\% CI & HO Holm $p$ & Status \\\\\n\\midrule\nGeneral closure (pooled) & $-0.66$ & $-0.39$ & $-0.86$ to $0.07$ & 0.147 & Not confirmed \\\\\nTurnover-residualised & $-0.40$ & $-0.11$ & $-0.56$ to $0.34$ & 0.635 & Not confirmed \\\\\nPersistent-neighbour & $-1.12$ & $-1.07$ & $-1.86$ to $-0.29$ & 0.015 & Confirmed \\\\\nBurt constraint & $+0.08$ & $+0.11$ & $0.02$ to $0.19$ & --- & Positive \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\multicolumn{6}{l}{\\scriptsize HO = Held-out fold.}\n\\end{tabularx}\n\\end{table}\n\nTable~\\ref{tab:closure} and Figure~\\ref{fig:closure} summarise these results. On the Held-out fold (a\ndevelopment-set estimate; the fold was used in pipeline development), general closure is not significant\n(Holm $p = 0.147$). Only persistent-neighbour closure, restricted to top-20 neighbours present in consecutive\nyears, is significant ($S = -1.07$, Holm $p = 0.015$). Burt constraint has the same positive sign on the\nHeld-out fold ($+0.11$, 95\\% CI 0.02 to 0.19), indicating that the lower closure before emergence is not\nBurt brokerage: concepts that later emerge sit in ego networks that are more constrained, not less.\n\nThe MeSH replication is directional under a sensitivity label ($D = -0.42$, Holm $p = 0.039$, $n = 29$),\nsame sign as the main pool, but under the primary label the MeSH effect is null ($D = -0.09$, Holm\n$p = 0.677$, $n = 15$).%\n\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-2/experiment-4}}\n\nStructural precursors add no predictive value for whether a concept will later show sustained uptake beyond\nfrequency, burst, degree and entropy baselines (logistic AUC 0.89 versus 0.88, delta $-0.010$, 95\\% CI\n$-0.045$ to 0.021).\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig3_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Pre-emergence closure on the held-out fold, by measure type. Each row shows the standardised mean\n  difference ($S$) between concepts that later show sustained uptake and matched controls. Points are estimates\n  and horizontal bars are 95\\% bootstrap confidence intervals. The dashed vertical line marks no effect\n  ($S = 0$), and Holm-corrected $p$-values are listed to the right of the first three rows. Only\n  persistent-neighbour closure (blue) survives Holm correction ($S = -1.07$, 95\\% CI $[-1.86, -0.29]$,\n  Holm $p = 0.015$). General closure (Holm $p = 0.147$) and turnover-residualised closure\n  (Holm $p = 0.635$) are shown in grey: they do not survive confirmation, and their intervals cross zero. Burt\n  constraint (orange) is positive ($S = 0.11$, 95\\% CI $[0.02, 0.19]$), which indicates that emerging concepts\n  sit in more constrained, not more brokered, ego networks.}\n  \\label{fig:closure}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\subsubsection{Comparison to related work}\n\\label{sec:rq1comparison}\n\nThe finding that emerging concepts show lower closure among their most stable co-word neighbours is consistent\nwith the observation of \\citet{Salatino2018} that new topics arise at the intersection of weakly connected\nparent areas, and with \\citeauthor{Chen2009}'s~\\citeyearpar{Chen2009} theory of structural variation in which\ntransformative work bridges structural holes. It is also consistent with the structural-holes\nliterature~\\citep{Burt2004}: concepts that later emerge connect across Leiden communities, and their\ncross-community pair excess is positive. The critical difference is that Burt constraint is higher, not lower.\nIn Burt's framework, brokerage means low constraint. Here the ego network is more redundant, not less; the\nopenness is confined to the top of the neighbourhood, while the broader ego network is dense. This pattern is\ncloser to what \\citet{Lin2021} describe as disconnection and discordance enabling new directions in science,\nand to \\citeauthor{Larson2017}'s~\\citeyearpar{Larson2017} finding that weak-tie diffusion in networks is not\nguaranteed to carry novel information.\n\nAmong Applied Network Science contributions, \\citet{Domenico2016} studied knowledge diaspora through\nsource-sink author flows, and \\citet{Cunningham2022} mapped author multidisciplinarity and disciplinary roles\nin field-of-study networks, finding that bridge authors between communities can accelerate knowledge transfer.\nOur structural analysis complements this by showing that concept-level network openness, not author-level\nbridging, precedes emergence. \\citet{Fontaine2023} traced the epistemic integration of AI into neuroscience,\nshowing how vocabulary overlap between fields facilitates absorption, a finding that connects directly to our\nhost-vocabulary result. \\citet{Doonan2019} found that community structure in co-inventor networks affects\ntime to first citation, paralleling our finding that community position shapes concept uptake.\n\\citet{Salatino2019} applied their Computer Science Ontology to classify research topics through network-based\ndetection, providing a taxonomy-grounded approach related to our co-word-network construction.\n\n\\subsection{Host-entry grafting}\n\\label{sec:rq2results}\n\n\\subsubsection{Experimental setup}\n\\label{sec:rq2setup}\n\nThe host-entry sample for the Screen fold comprises 1,544 events across 140 concept clusters (co-primary\nspecification). Entry is predominantly a package: 70\\% of partner tags are non-native origin companions, and\nonly 1.8\\% are native grafts (host share above 50\\%). The mean host-vocabulary share is 0.043 (SD 0.055). The\nHeld-out fold has 972 events across 74 concept clusters. The MeSH population has 2,171 events across 160\nconcept clusters.\n\n\\subsubsection{Main result}\n\\label{sec:rq2main}\n\n\\begin{table}[!htbp]\n\\centering\n\\caption{Host-entry grafting: pre-registered test. IRR/SD = incidence-rate ratio per one standard deviation\nof host-vocabulary share. CT = co-transfer. G = concept clusters. IVW = inverse-variance weighted.}\n\\label{tab:grafting}\n\\small\n\\begin{tabularx}{\\linewidth}{l l c c c c c c}\n\\toprule\nSpecification & Fold & IRR/SD & 95\\% CI & $p$ & CT $p$ & $N$ & $G$ \\\\\n\\midrule\nCo-primary & Screen & 1.30 & 1.16--1.45 & ${<}\\,0.001$ & 0.48 & 1,544 & 140 \\\\\nCo-primary & Held-out & 1.19 & 1.06--1.33 & 0.004 & 0.60 & 972 & 74 \\\\\nPrimary (strict FE) & Held-out & 0.98 & 0.70--1.37 & 0.91 & 0.22 & 250 & 30 \\\\\nCo-primary & MeSH & 1.23 & 1.12--1.36 & ${<}\\,0.001$ & 0.053 & 2,171 & 160 \\\\\nPrimary & MeSH & 1.32 & 1.10--1.60 & 0.004 & 0.46 & 1,004 & 122 \\\\\nCo-primary (IVW) & All three & 1.26 & 1.17--1.36 & ${<}\\,0.001$ & --- & --- & --- \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabularx}\n\\end{table}\n\nTable~\\ref{tab:grafting} presents the pre-registered test. On the independent MeSH biomedical population, a\none-standard-deviation increase in host-vocabulary share raises newcomer uptake by 23\\% (co-primary IRR 1.23,\n95\\% CI 1.12 to 1.36, $p < 0.001$; primary IRR 1.32, 95\\% CI 1.10 to 1.60, $p = 0.004$; pre-registered\nverdict: REPLICATED). The main-arm folds, both used in\npipeline development (event counts, population sizes and gating decisions were computed on both folds before\noutcomes were read), give concordant development-set estimates: Screen co-primary IRR 1.30 (95\\% CI 1.16 to\n1.45); Held-out co-primary IRR 1.19 (95\\% CI 1.06 to 1.33, wild-cluster bootstrap $p = 0.012$,\nnativeness-permutation $p = 0.026$). Heterogeneity between Screen and Held-out is not significant\n($p = 0.25$). The inverse-variance weighted pooled estimate across all three folds is 1.26 (95\\% CI 1.17\nto 1.36, $I^2 = 0$). Co-transfer is null across all folds and specifications\n(Figure~\\ref{fig:grafting}).\n\nThe fully saturated primary specification on the Held-out fold is inconclusive (IRR 0.98, 95\\% CI 0.70 to\n1.37) because it retains only 250 of 972 events with 30 concept clusters; this was declared underpowered in\nadvance (minimum detectable effect IRR 1.30).\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig4_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Host-vocabulary effect on five-year newcomer uptake across folds and specifications. Each row gives\n  the PPML incidence-rate ratio (IRR) per one standard deviation of host-vocabulary share, on a log axis;\n  horizontal bars are 95\\% concept-clustered confidence intervals, and the dashed vertical line marks\n  IRR $= 1$ (no effect). Filled circles are the co-primary specification (concept, entry-year and host fixed\n  effects) and open circles the primary specification with concept$\\times$year and host$\\times$year fixed\n  effects. Blue marks the OpenAlex screen and sealed held-out folds, green the independent MeSH replication,\n  and the amber diamond the inverse-variance weighted (IVW) pooled co-primary estimate. The co-primary effect\n  is significant on all three folds (screen IRR 1.30 [1.16, 1.45], held-out 1.19 [1.06, 1.33], MeSH 1.23\n  [1.12, 1.36]), and the pooled estimate is 1.26 [1.17, 1.36]. The primary specification is inconclusive on\n  the held-out fold (IRR 0.98 [0.70, 1.37], 30 clusters, $p = 0.91$) but significant on MeSH (IRR 1.32\n  [1.10, 1.60]). Grey diamonds are the co-transfer regressor from the co-primary models. Its intervals\n  include 1 on every fold ($p = 0.48$, $0.60$ and $0.053$). The right-hand columns list each estimate with\n  its 95\\% CI and $p$-value.}\n  \\label{fig:grafting}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\paragraph{Robustness.} The co-primary effect holds in 20 of 26 robustness variants on the Screen fold (IRR\nrange 1.11 to 1.56 among significant rows). All seven pre-specified robustness rows on the Held-out fold are\nsignificant. Nativeness-permutation placebos are centred on 1.0 (co-primary $p = 0.002$ Screen, 0.026\nHeld-out, 0.010 MeSH). The cluster-robust variance estimator mildly over-rejects at the null (size 10.5\\% on\nMeSH simulation), so $p$-values should be read alongside the wild-cluster and permutation results.\n\n\\subsubsection{Mechanism decomposition}\n\\label{sec:rq2mechanism}\n\n\\paragraph{Extensive versus intensive margins.} The host-vocabulary effect operates through both the extensive\nmargin, meaning whether any newcomer uptake starts, and the intensive margin, meaning the count of newcomer\npapers given that uptake started. The inverse-variance weighted extensive-margin effect is $+6.4$ percentage\npoints per standard deviation (95\\% CI 4.8 to 8.1, randomisation-$t$ $p < 0.001$), approximately a 13\\%\nincrease relative to the base rate of 51\\%. The inverse-variance weighted intensive-margin incidence-rate ratio\nper standard deviation is 1.18 (95\\% CI 1.10 to 1.27). The extensive share of the total effect is 0.38\n(95\\% CI 0.21 to 0.55; Figure~\\ref{fig:margins}).\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig5_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Decomposition of the host-vocabulary effect into extensive and intensive margins across the screen,\n  held-out and MeSH folds. Blue circles show per-fold estimates, vermillion diamonds the inverse-variance-weighted\n  (IVW) pooled estimate, and horizontal bars 95\\% confidence intervals. (a)~Extensive margin:\n  linear-probability-model effect of a one-standard-deviation increase in host-vocabulary share on the\n  probability of any newcomer uptake, in percentage points per SD (dashed line: no effect). The pooled effect\n  is 6.43~pp (95\\% CI 4.76 to 8.11). (b)~Intensive margin: PPML incidence-rate ratio per SD conditional on\n  uptake, on a log axis (dashed line: IRR $= 1$). The pooled IRR is 1.183 (95\\% CI 1.104 to 1.267). All three\n  folds are positive on both margins, and every fold interval excludes the null. (c)~Share of the total effect:\n  the extensive margin accounts for 38\\% (95\\% CI 21\\% to 55\\%, black whisker) and the intensive margin for\n  the remaining 62\\%.}\n  \\label{fig:margins}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\paragraph{Host-specific versus generic accessibility.} Adding generality controls (subfield entropy and log\nfrequency of entry partners) to the co-primary model retains 97\\% of the host-vocabulary coefficient\n(inverse-variance weighted retention 0.97, 95\\% CI 0.81 to 1.10), and the Balassa-index lift measure is also\nsignificant (inverse-variance weighted IRR per standard deviation 1.34, 95\\% CI 1.23 to 1.46). The\nhost-vocabulary gradient is not reducible to generic concept accessibility. However, within fixed effects the\nBalassa-index lift measure has a correlation of 0.997 with the log of the continuous host-vocabulary share,\nso the lift leg of this test is weak: the two measures carry nearly the same within-unit information, and the\nlift result should be interpreted as confirming the continuous share rather than adding independent evidence\nfor host-specificity.\n\n\\paragraph{No origin-field boundary.} The Wald test for equality of the host-vocabulary effect across\norigin-field groups (Physics and Astronomy, Computer Science, other) is null ($p = 0.64$, label-permutation\n$p = 0.77$). Physics and Astronomy concepts, whose host-vocabulary coefficient is individually non-significant\n(IRR 1.18, 95\\% CI 0.93 to 1.50), fall within sampling variation of the other groups.\n\n\\subsubsection{Diffusion typology and expansion-before-diffusion ordering}\n\\label{sec:rq2typology}\n\nA data-derived typology based on multivariate dynamic time warping of three diversity channels (rarefied\nShannon entropy, Rao-Stirling diversity~\\citep{Stirling2007} and active subfield count) yields a stable\ntwo-cluster solution ($k$-medoids, Hennig bootstrap~\\citep{Hennig2007} minimum Jaccard 0.86):\n\\textbf{localised} ($n = 136$, low entropy and few active subfields) and \\textbf{broad from the start}\n($n = 66$, high entropy from early years). Finer clusterings are unstable ($k = 3$ Jaccard 0.60). The typology\ndoes not separate outcomes better than an entropy-only baseline after residualising on early volume.\n\nAmong concepts exhibiting both a co-word-network expansion onset and a disciplinary-diffusion onset, expansion\nprecedes diffusion in 25 of 26 pooled main-arm cases (proportion 0.96, 95\\% CI 0.81 to 1.00, year-shuffle\nnull 0.62, $p = 0.004$), though only 8.6\\% of concepts have both onsets observable. On MeSH, 9 of 13 show\nexpansion first (not different from the null, $p = 0.43$).\n\n\\subsubsection{Adopter-level mechanism}\n\\label{sec:rq2adopter}\n\nAdopters, defined as authors who publish a concept paper in the host subfield within the five-year outcome\nwindow, are more likely to have prior corpus exposure to the concept's entry partners than matched non-adopters\nfrom the same host subfield (conditional logistic regression: OR 3.09, prevalence 0.79 versus 0.61; 95\\% CI\n2.32 to 4.28; 1,013 matched strata, 422 entries, 109 concepts). Exposure to frequency-matched\nnegative-control concepts is negatively associated (OR 0.62), and the placebo control using partners of a\ndifferent concept's entry into the same host is also below 1 (OR 0.72), showing specificity to the concept's\nown partners.\n\nDecomposing partners into three vocabulary classes --- FOREIGN (origin vocabulary, host share below 5\\%),\nADJACENT (5\\% to 30\\%) and NATIVE (host vocabulary, above 30\\%) --- enrichment follows a gradient: FOREIGN\npartners OR 2.88, ADJACENT partners OR 1.91, NATIVE partners OR 1.47. Adopters who pick up a concept in a new\nfield are most enriched for prior exposure to its origin-vocabulary partners, consistent with the\nabsorptive-capacity framework~\\citep{Cohen1990} in which an individual's ability to recognise and assimilate\nexternal knowledge depends on prior familiarity with that knowledge. This Screen-fold result is not\nindependently confirmed.\n\n\\subsubsection{Comparison to related work}\n\\label{sec:rq2comparison}\n\nOur host-vocabulary measure is closest to the ideational embeddedness of \\citet{Cheng2023}, who found that a\nconcept's fit with existing traditions raises its yearly article count. Their measure is a global property of\nthe concept (mean cosine similarity of all its neighbours in a word2vec embedding), whereas ours is\nentry-specific: measured at the level of each concept-subfield-year event, with concept and host fixed effects\nabsorbing concept-level confounds. Co-transfer, the natural competitor, is null. This extends the principle\nthat relatedness predicts diversification, documented in economic\ngeography~\\citep{Boschma2014, Hidalgo2018}, to the level of individual concept-entry events.\n\nAmong Applied Network Science papers, our work engages most directly with the source-sink analysis of\nknowledge diaspora by \\citet{Domenico2016}, which modelled author flows as diffusion on a bipartite field\nnetwork. Our approach replaces author flows with concept-vocabulary composition at the entry point, and finds\nthat vocabulary, not people, predicts rooting. \\citet{Cunningham2022} documented how multidisciplinary authors\noccupy bridging positions in field-of-study networks, a role that might facilitate the host-vocabulary\ncomposition we measure. \\citet{Fontaine2023} showed that vocabulary overlap between AI and neuroscience\nfacilitated epistemic integration, and our quantitative test provides the micro-level mechanism consistent\nwith their macro-level observation. \\citet{Holmgren2023} developed multilevel alluvial methods for mapping\nchange in higher-order networks, related to the alluvial community tracking we use. \\citet{Medeuov2021}\nappraised discrepancies in semantic networks, finding that endogenous reinforcement within a community is\nweak while exogenous diffusion is predictable, consistent with our expansion-before-diffusion ordering.\n\\citet{Liew2016} applied multiplex network analysis to map disciplinary knowledge flows.\n\n\\subsubsection{Representative cases}\n\\label{sec:rq2cases}\n\nFour medoid cases from the typology clusters illustrate the host-vocabulary gradient at the concept level\n(Figure~\\ref{fig:cases}).\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig6_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Four representative cases of the host-vocabulary gradient. Each panel shows one concept, and each\n  horizontal bar is one of its host entries in the co-primary sample, labelled by host subfield and entry year\n  and sorted by host-vocabulary share (x-axis, fraction). Green bars are rooted entries and grey bars are\n  non-rooted entries. The dashed line marks the mean share of the non-rooted entries, and rooted bars are\n  annotated with their share and number of newcomer papers. (a)~Wireless backhaul (broad, CS): 14 entries, one\n  rooted (Aerospace Engineering 2008, share 0.084, 6 newcomers) against a non-rooted mean of 0.021.\n  (b)~Einstein--Podolsky--Rosen (EPR) steering (broad, Physics): 7 entries, one rooted (Artificial Intelligence\n  2011, 0.142, 37 newcomers; co-transfer 0) against a non-rooted mean of 0.027. (c)~Locally repairable code\n  (localised, CS): a single co-primary entry, rooted (0.056, 3 newcomers), so there is no within-concept\n  contrast. (d)~Holographic QCD (localised, Physics): 5 entries, none rooted (mean 0.041; three have\n  co-transfer 1.0), including an AMO Physics entry at 0.132 that did not take root. In (a) and (b), the rooted\n  entry has a higher host-vocabulary share than every non-rooted entry of the same concept. The panels are\n  descriptive, so no intervals are drawn.}\n  \\label{fig:cases}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\paragraph{Wireless backhaul} (broad type, Computer Science, first appeared 2006). Broad from its first year,\nsplitting between Computer Networks and Electrical Engineering. By 2022 seven subfields are active. Of 14 host\nentries in the co-primary sample, only one is rooted (Aerospace Engineering in 2008, host-vocabulary share\n0.084, 6 newcomer papers). The 13 non-rooted entries average a host-vocabulary share of 0.021 and arrive as\norigin packages (co-transfer 0.6 to 1.0). Rooted-minus-unrooted host-vocabulary share: $+0.062$.\n\n\\paragraph{Einstein--Podolsky--Rosen steering} (broad type, Physics, first appeared 2011). Of 7 co-primary\nentries, one is rooted (Artificial Intelligence in 2011, host-vocabulary share 0.142, co-transfer 0, 37\nnewcomer papers). The 6 non-rooted entries average 0.027 with co-transfer at or above 0.55. Rooted-minus-unrooted:\n$+0.115$. A broad-type label can hide a concept whose cross-disciplinary integration rests on a single\nwell-anchored entry.\n\n\\paragraph{Locally repairable code} (localised type, Computer Science, first appeared 2013). Stays at 84\\% to\n96\\% in Computer Networks for its life. Has only 1 co-primary entry (AI in 2013, host-vocabulary share 0.056,\nrooted). Demonstrates rooting without broad occupancy.\n\n\\paragraph{Holographic QCD} (localised type, Physics, first appeared 2006). Stays at 95\\% to 97\\% in Nuclear\nand High Energy Physics. Its 5 co-primary entries are all non-rooted, averaging 0.041, with three having\nco-transfer of 1.0: pure origin packages. No entry is rooted. A locally concentrated concept whose excursions\nare packaged imports that do not take root.\n\n\\subsection{Community roles and bridging}\n\\label{sec:community}\n\nLeiden community roles (five-seed agreement 97.2\\%) partition concepts into four categories: bridge (0.61),\nother (0.33), stayer (0.03) and migrant (0.02). Emerging concepts are peripheral or connector nodes in the\nGuimera--Amaral cartography~\\citep{Guimera2005a} (peripheral 0.49, connector 0.40, kinless 0.10, no hubs).\nLagged roles do not robustly predict host-subfield entry (bridge odds ratio 0.64, 95\\% CI 0.38 to 1.08).\n\nMost emerging concepts act as bridges between Leiden communities in the co-word network (early-bridging share\n0.70 in the main pool versus 0.59 in MeSH, difference $+0.11$, 95\\% CI 0.02 to 0.20), but this bridging role\nis common and non-discriminating.\n\n\\section{Discussion}\n\\label{sec:discussion}\n\n\\subsection{What host-vocabulary composition tells us}\n\nThe central finding is that a concept's first partners in a new subfield carry information about whether that\nconcept will subsequently be adopted by newcomer scientists in the host field. The host-vocabulary share, a\nratio measuring how much of each partner's prior work belongs to the host subfield, predicts five-year newcomer\nuptake in a pre-registered design replicated on an independent MeSH biomedical population (verdict: REPLICATED),\nwith concordant development-set estimates on the main-arm folds.\n\nThis result complements the absorptive-capacity framework~\\citep{Cohen1990}. At the entry level,\nhost-vocabulary composition facilitates uptake by newcomers who may not be experts in the concept's origin\nfield. At the adopter level, the individuals who actually pick up the concept are enriched for prior exposure\nto the concept's origin-vocabulary partners (OR 3.09, prevalence 0.79 versus 0.61; Screen fold, not\nindependently confirmed), consistent with the proposition that recognising external knowledge requires prior\nfamiliarity with it. These two findings operate at different scales: host-native partners lower the barrier for\nthe field, but the individuals who cross it already speak the origin language.\n\n\\subsection{What structural openness tells us}\n\nThe persistent-neighbour closure result (significant on the Held-out development fold, $S = -1.07$, Holm\n$p = 0.015$) indicates that concepts whose top associates do not close into triads from year to year are more\nlikely to show sustained uptake. General closure is not significant on the Held-out fold. Burt constraint is\npositive, meaning the ego network is redundant, not brokered. The picture is of open, fast-renewing connections\namong a concept's most strongly associated terms within a dense wider ego network, rather than brokerage across\na structural hole. This is consistent with the finding of \\citet{Lin2021} that disconnection and discordance\nseed new directions.\n\n\\subsection{Null findings and what they bound}\n\nSeveral pre-registered hypotheses were not supported. Co-transfer, defined as arriving with origin companions,\nis null in all specifications and populations, meaning that the composition of entry matters but the\nimported-package channel does not. The breadth-prediction screen (does openness predict how many new subfields\na concept will reach?) found no effect beyond growth and level baselines.%\n\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-3/experiment-6}}\nThe link between pre-emergence closure and later host-entry composition is null (partial correlation 0.025\nScreen, 0.053 Held-out, both confidence intervals including zero), meaning that network openness and vocabulary\ncomposition operate independently rather than through a shared mechanism.\n\n\\section{Limitations}\n\\label{sec:limitations}\n\n\\paragraph{Main-arm folds used in development.} The fold labelled Held-out was used during pipeline\ndevelopment: event counts, population sizes and gating decisions were computed on both the Screen and Held-out\nfolds before grafting outcomes were read. Estimates on both main-arm folds are therefore development-set\nestimates, not true held-out confirmations. The independent evidence for the host-vocabulary effect comes from\nthe MeSH replication (verdict: REPLICATED).\n\n\\paragraph{Population bias.} The concept pool is dominated by physics, physical-sciences and computer-science\nconcepts from arXiv. The MeSH population covers only biomedicine-to-biomedicine entries. Generalisation to\nsocial sciences, humanities or engineering is untested.\n\n\\paragraph{Primary specification underpowered.} The fully saturated specification with concept-by-year and\nhost-by-year fixed effects, which absorbs more confounding than the co-primary, is inconclusive on the Held-out\nfold (IRR 0.98, 30 clusters). The independent MeSH replication and the development-set estimates rest on the\nco-primary specification, which leaves more residual variation.\n\n\\paragraph{Single-paper entries.} 87\\% of co-primary Screen events involve a single entry-year paper. The\npooled multi-team effect is positive (IRR 1.28, 95\\% CI 1.11 to 1.48), but the Held-out alone is underpowered\nfor this test.\n\n\\paragraph{Binary establishment null.} The host-vocabulary share predicts the count of newcomer papers and the\nprobability that any newcomer uptake occurs, but binary establishment (at least five newcomer papers in at least\nthree of five years) is null on the Held-out fold ($p = 0.16$). The effect is graded, not threshold-based.\n\n\\paragraph{Cluster-robust inference.} The cluster-robust variance estimator rejects 10\\% to 11\\% of null\nshuffles in simulation (target 5\\%). Wild-cluster bootstrap and permutation tests give consistent results\n(Held-out wild $p = 0.012$, permutation $p = 0.026$), but the standard $p$-values should not be taken at\nface value.\n\n\\paragraph{Host-specificity caveat.} The Balassa-index lift measure used to test host-specificity has a\nwithin-fixed-effect correlation of 0.997 with the log of the continuous host-vocabulary share. The lift test\nconfirms the continuous measure rather than providing independent evidence.\n\n\\paragraph{Screen-fold adopter evidence.} The adopter-level enrichment (OR 3.09) is Screen-fold only, not\nindependently confirmed. The design cannot separate absorptive capacity from topical proximity.\n\n\\paragraph{Closure Held-out caveats.} The Held-out fold was used in pipeline development, so the closure\nresult is a development-set estimate. Additionally, the Held-out matching falls back to Screen controls for\n17 of 25 unique controls, so the estimator is not fully control-side independent. The MeSH closure result is\ndirectional under the sensitivity label but null under the primary label.\n\n\\section{Conclusions}\n\\label{sec:conclusions}\n\nWhen a new scientific concept enters a disciplinary subfield, the vocabulary composition of its initial\npartners predicts whether newcomer scientists in that field will subsequently adopt it. This host-vocabulary\neffect, replicated on 191 independent MeSH biomedical concepts (co-primary IRR 1.23, verdict REPLICATED)\nwith concordant main-arm development-set estimates (Screen IRR 1.30, Held-out IRR 1.19), is host-specific\n--- though the Balassa-index lift leg of this test is near-collinear with the continuous share\n(within-fixed-effect $r = 0.997$) --- operates through both the extensive and intensive margins, and does\nnot vary by the concept's origin field. Co-transfer of origin companions is null.\n\nThe complementary structural finding, that persistent-neighbour closure is lower before sustained uptake\n(Held-out development-set estimate $S = -1.07$, Holm $p = 0.015$) while Burt constraint is higher, provides\nthe network context: emerging concepts sit in locally open, fast-renewing neighbourhoods that span multiple\ncommunities but are not brokered in Burt's sense.\n\nThese results bear on how knowledge transfer is evaluated and supported. Policies and platforms that facilitate\ncross-disciplinary research might benefit from attending to the vocabulary composition of a concept's first\nappearance in a new field, rather than only to the mobility of authors who carry it.\n\nFuture work should extend the concept pool beyond the physical and computational sciences, test whether the\nhost-vocabulary gradient holds for social-science and humanities concepts, and design an experiment to separate\nabsorptive capacity from topical proximity at the adopter level.\n\n\\section*{Declarations}\n\n\\paragraph{Funding.} Not applicable.\n\n\\paragraph{Conflicts of interest.} The authors declare no conflicts of interest.\n\n\\paragraph{Availability of data and materials.} All data derive from OpenAlex, an open scholarly metadata\nindex. The concept pool, verified work lists and analysis code are available in the project repository.\n\n\\paragraph{Code availability.} All analysis code is available in the project repository.\n\n\\paragraph{Keywords.} Knowledge diffusion, emerging concepts, co-word network, host vocabulary,\ncross-disciplinary integration, applied network science, scientometrics, concept emergence.\n\n\\bibliographystyle{plainnat}\n\\bibliography{references}\n\n\\end{document}\n", "numLines": 697, "startLine": 1, "totalLines": 697}}

The extensive margin (whether any uptake starts) accounts for 38% of the total effect (95% CI 21% to 55%): the pooled effect is +6.4 percentage points per SD (95% CI 4.8 to 8.1), approximately a 13% increase relative to the 51% base rate. The intensive margin (count of newcomer papers given uptake started) accounts for the remaining 62%, with a pooled IRR of 1.18 (95% CI 1.10 to 1.27).</p>\n403:<p>The host-vocabulary gradient is host-specific. Adding generality controls retains 97% of the coefficient (IVW retention 0.97, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.10). The Balassa-index lift measure is also significant (IVW IRR 1.34, 95% CI 1.23 to 1.46), though its within-fixed-effect correlation with the log of the continuous share is 0.997, so the lift test confirms the continuous measure rather than adding independent evidence (<a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-5/evaluation-7\">code</a>). The Wald test for origin-field dependence is null (p = 0.64).</p>\n406:<p>On the Held-out fold (a development-set estimate), only persistent-neighbour closure survives Holm correction: S = &#x2212;1.07, 95% CI &#x2212;1.86 to &#x2212;0.29, Holm p = 0.015. General closure is not significant (Holm p = 0.147). Turnover-residualised closure is not significant (Holm p = 0.635). Burt constraint is positive (S = +0.11, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.19), indicating that emerging concepts sit in more constrained, not more brokered, ego networks (<a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-3/experiment-5\">code</a>, <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-4/evaluation-3\">held-out check</a>).</p>\n408:<p>The MeSH replication of closure is directional under a sensitivity label (D = &#x2212;0.42, Holm p = 0.039, n = 29) but null under the primary label (D = &#x2212;0.09, Holm p = 0.677, n = 15) (<a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-2/experiment-4\">code</a>). Structural precursors add no predictive value for sustained uptake beyond frequency, burst, degree and entropy baselines (logistic AUC 0.89 versus 0.88).</p>\n411:<p>Adopters are more likely to have prior corpus exposure to the concept's entry partners than matched non-adopters (conditional logistic regression: OR 3.09, prevalence 0.79 versus 0.61; 95% CI 2.32 to 4.28; 1,013 matched strata, 422 entries, 109 concepts; Screen fold, not independently confirmed) (<a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-4/evaluation-5\">code</a>). Enrichment follows a vocabulary gradient: FOREIGN partners OR 2.88, ADJACENT OR 1.91, NATIVE OR 1.47.</p>\n414:<p>A data-derived two-type typology (localised, n = 136, vs. broad from the start, n = 66; k-medoids, bootstrap minimum Jaccard 0.86) is stable, though it does not separate outcomes better than an entropy-only baseline. Among concepts with both observable onsets, expansion precedes diffusion in 25 of 26 pooled main-arm cases (proportion 0.96, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.00, p = 0.004) (<a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-3/experiment-8\">code</a>, <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-4/evaluation-4\">unseen data check</a>).</p>\n417:<p>Co-transfer is null in all specifications and populations. The breadth-prediction screen (does openness predict how many subfields a concept reaches?) found no effect beyond growth and level baselines (<a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-3/experiment-6\">code</a>). The link between pre-emergence closure and later host-entry composition is null (partial correlation 0.025 Screen, 0.053 Held-out, both CIs including zero).</p>\n518:<li><a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-1/dataset-4\">Code: Labelled science phrases and new-term def jload(p):
    return json.loads(Path(p).read_text())


def ptr(obj, pointer):
    for part in pointer.strip("/").split("/"):
        obj = obj[int(part)] if isinstance(obj, list) else obj[part]
    return obj


def csv_rows(p):
    with open(p, newline="") as f:
        return list(csv.DictReader(f))


def fnum(x):
    if x is None or x == "":
        return None
    v = float(x)
    return None if math.isnan(v) else v


def r(x, n=6):
    return None if x is None else round(float(x), n)


def dump(name, obj):
    (OUT / f"{name}.json").write_text(json.dumps(obj, separators=(",", ":"), ensure_ascii=False))
    print(name, (OUT / f"{name}.json").stat().st_size, "bytes")


def fmt_p(p):
    if p < 0.001:
        return "<0.001"
    if p < 0.1:
        return f"{p:.3f}"
    return f"{p:.2f}"

                        ("closure_persist", "Persistent-neighbour closure", "pooled panel"), ("constraint", "Burt constraint", "event study")]:
    if est == "pooled panel":
        s = pp[row]
        scr = fnum(s["coef_screen"]); se_s = fnum(s["se_screen"])
        item = dict(row=row, label=label, estimator=est,
                    screen=dict(S=r(scr), lo=r(scr - 1.96 * se_s), hi=r(scr + 1.96 * se_s), ci_note="coef ± 1.96 SE"),
                    heldout=dict(S=r(s["coef_heldout"]), lo=r(s["ci_heldout_lo"]), hi=r(s["ci_heldout_hi"])))
    else:
        s = es[row]
        item = dict(row=row, label=label, estimator=est,
                    screen=dict(S=r(s["S_screen"]), lo=r(s["ci_screen_lo"]), hi=r(s["ci_screen_hi"])),
                    heldout=dict(S=r(s["S_heldout"]), lo=r(s["ci_heldout_lo"]), hi=r(s["ci_heldout_hi"])))
    t = r1["tests"][row]
    item.update(holm=r(t["p_one_holm"]), decision=t["decision"])

            "closure_persist": ("-1.12", "-1.07", "-1.86", "-0.29", "0.015"), "constraint": ("0.08", "0.11", "0.02", "0.19", None)}
for it in closure:
    ps, ph, plo, phi, holm = paper_cl[it["row"]]
    got = (f"{it['screen']['S']:.2f}", f"{it['heldout']['S']:.2f}", f"{it['heldout']['lo']:.2f}", f"{it['heldout']['hi']:.2f}")
    it["paper"] = dict(screen=ps.replace("-", "−"), heldout=ph.replace("-", "−"),
                       ci=f"{plo} to {phi}".replace("-", "−"), holm=holm)
    if got != (ps, ph, plo, phi):
        it["paper_note"] = f"file values {got}; the paper prints {(ps, ph, plo, phi)}"
        print("closure display differs:", it["row"], got, (ps, ph, plo, phi))
    if holm:
        assert f"{it['holm']:.3f}" == holm
dump("closure", dict(rows=closure, n_onsets=None, status=r1["status"],
                     src="evaluation_3/results/tables/r1_pooled_panel_screen_vs_heldout.csv; r1_event_study_screen_vs_heldout.csv; results/r1/r1_summary.json"))

print("stepper event", step["event"])

<a class="skip" href="#main">Skip to main content</a>
<header class="site">
  <div class="wrap">
    <div class="kicker">Explorable companion to the paper</div>
    <h1>Host vocabulary predicts whether new scientific concepts take root across disciplinary boundaries</h1>
    <p class="byline">The paper carries no author line. Every chart below is drawn from the run's recorded output files.</p>
    <div class="links">
      <a class="btn primary" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new@fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/paper.pdf">Read the paper (PDF)</a>
      <a class="btn" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new@fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/report.pdf">Read the full research report</a>
      <a class="btn" href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq">Code repository</a>
    </div>
  </div>
</header>
<nav class="sec" aria-label="Sections">
  <ol>
    <li><a href="#finding">The finding</a></li>
    <li><a href="#method">How it works</a></li>
    <li><a href="#evidence">Explore the evidence</a></li>
    <li><a href="#tryit">Try it</a></li>
    <li><a href="#fails">Where it fails</a></li>
    <li><a href="#sources">Sources &amp; glossary</a></li>
  </ol>
</nav>

<main id="main">
<!-- ============================================================ FINDING -->
<section class="block" id="finding" aria-labelledby="h-finding">
<div class="wrap finding">
  <div>
    <h2 id="h-finding">The finding</h2>
    <p class="q"><strong>The question.</strong> When a scientific concept first appears in a subfield that is not its home, what decides whether researchers in that field take it up?</p>
    <p>The study follows every <button class="term" data-term="entry">host-entry event</button> of 426 emerging concepts across 462,812 OpenAlex works: the first year a concept appears in a non-origin subfield with at least five co-occurring partner terms. For each entry it measures the <button class="term" data-term="share">host-vocabulary share</button> of those partners and counts the papers written about the concept in that subfield by <button class="term" data-term="newcomer">newcomer authors</button> over the next five years.</p>
    <div class="bignum" id="bignum" aria-describedby="bignum-cap"></div>
    <p class="bignum-cap" id="bignum-cap"></p>
    <p><strong>The answer.</strong> Entries whose first partners already belong to the host's vocabulary draw more newcomers. On the independent <button class="term" data-term="mesh">MeSH population</button>, a one-standard-deviation higher share raises newcomer uptake by 23% (pre-registered and replicated). Development-set estimates on the <button class="term" data-term="screen">Screen</button> and <button class="term" data-term="heldout">Held-out</button> folds agree. The competing idea, that concepts root when they arrive with their origin companions (<button class="term" data-term="ct">co-transfer</button>), is null everywhere.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="card" id="forest-card">
    <p class="q"><strong>Does it hold on every population?</strong> Each row is a pre-registered <button class="term" data-term="ppml">PPML</button> estimate: the <button class="term" data-term="irr">IRR</button> per SD of the regressor. The dashed line at 1 means no effect.</p>
    <div class="seg" role="tablist" aria-label="What to compare" id="forest-tabs">
      <button role="tab" id="tab-folds" aria-selected="true" aria-controls="forest-panel" data-tab="folds">Across folds</button>
      <button role="tab" id="tab-origin" aria-selected="false" aria-controls="forest-panel" data-tab="origin" tabindex="-1">By origin field</button>
      <button role="tab" id="tab-placebo" aria-selected="false" aria-controls="forest-panel" data-tab="placebo" tabindex="-1">Placebo hosts</button>
    </div>
    <div id="forest-panel" role="tabpanel" aria-labelledby="tab-folds" style="margin-top:12px">
      <div class="controls" id="forest-controls">
        <div class="seg" role="radiogroup" aria-label="Model specification">
          <label><input type="radio" name="spec" value="co" checked>Co-primary FE</label>
          <label><input type="radio" name="spec" value="pri">Primary FE (stricter)</label>
        </div>
        <label><input type="checkbox" id="show-ct" checked>Show co-transfer</label>
      </div>
      <div class="chart" id="forest-chart"></div>
      <div class="legend" id="forest-legend"></div>
    </div>
    <p class="takeaway" id="forest-take" aria-live="polite"></p>
  </div>
</div>
</section>

<!-- ============================================================ METHOD -->
<section class="block" id="method" aria-labelledby="h-method">
<div class="wrap">
  <h2 id="h-method">How it works: one real entry, stage by stage</h2>
  <p class="q prose"><strong>How does a single entry become a data point?</strong> The stepper follows <em>Einstein–Podolsky–Rosen steering</em> into Artificial Intelligence in 2011, one of the paper's four representative cases, with the values the run recorded at each stage. Use the buttons, the stage markers, or the left and right arrow keys.</p>
  <div class="stepper card" id="stepper" tabindex="-1">
    <div class="pipe" id="pipe" role="group" aria-label="Method stages"></div>
    <div class="stepnav">
      <button type="button" id="step-prev">&larr; Previous</button>
      <button type="button" id="step-next">Next &rarr;</button>
      <span class="stepcount" id="step-count"></span>
    </div>
    <div aria-live="polite" id="step-live" class="sr"></div>
    <h3 id="step-title" style="margin-top:.2em"></h3>
    <div class="stage">
      <div><h4>What goes in</h4><div id="step-in"></div></div>
      <div><h4>What is done</h4><div id="step-do"></div></div>
      <div><h4>What comes out</h4><div id="step-out"></div></div>
    </div>
    <div class="chart" id="step-chart"></div>
    <p class="why" id="step-why"></p>
  </div>
  <figure>
    <img src="figures/fig1_v0.jpg" alt="Study design in four panels: (a) an arXiv concept pool of 426 concepts split into screen and held-out folds plus a MeSH check population of 191 concepts, drawn from 462,812 OpenAlex works; (b) a co-word network with Leiden communities; (c) the matched event study comparing closure before sustained uptake with controls; (d) host-entry grafting, where a concept moves from its origin subfield into a host subfield and the host-vocabulary share of its partners predicts five-year newcomer uptake." loading="lazy" width="3840" height="1648">
    <figcaption><strong>Paper Figure 1.</strong> Overview of the study design. (a) Data: an outcome-blind arXiv concept pool of 426 emerging scientific concepts, split into a screen fold (247) and a held-out fold (119), and an independent MeSH biomedical check population of 191 concepts. Both are drawn from 462,812 OpenAlex works. (b) Co-word network: yearly co-word snapshots (25 snapshots, ~27k nodes, ~84k edges) with Leiden communities; the schematic shows three colour-coded communities. (c) RQ1, emergence precursors: a matched event study compares closure measures in the pre-onset window (shaded) between concepts showing sustained uptake (blue, rising after onset) and controls (grey, flat). (d) RQ2, host-entry grafting: a concept enters a non-origin host subfield (light blue → light green region). Its partner terms are either host-native (dark green) or from the origin vocabulary (light blue). The host-vocabulary share (orange) is the exposure in a pre-registered PPML regression with concept-clustered standard errors predicting 5-year newcomer uptake. The timelines and bars in (c) and (d) are schematic and carry no data values.</figcaption>
  </figure>
</div>
</section>

<!-- ============================================================ EVIDENCE -->
<section class="block" id="evidence" aria-labelledby="h-evidence">
<div class="wrap">
  <h2 id="h-evidence">Explore the evidence</h2>
  <p class="prose">The views below read the per-entry records the run saved: 1,740 Screen entries, 1,097 Held-out entries and 2,249 MeSH entries with at least five partners. The regressions keep 1,544, 972 and 2,171 of them once the fixed effects drop cells with no variation, so counts here are a little larger than the model samples.</p>

  <h3 id="h-concept">Within one concept, which entries took root?</h3>
  <div class="card">
    <p class="q"><strong>Does the gradient show up inside a single concept?</strong> Each bar is one host entry of the chosen concept, sorted by host-vocabulary share. Green bars are <button class="term" data-term="rooted">rooted</button> entries.</p>
    <div class="controls">
      <label for="concept-sel">Concept</label>
      <select id="concept-sel"></select>
      <span class="seg" role="group" aria-label="Paper cases" id="case-btns"></span>
    </div>
    <div class="chart" id="concept-chart"></div>
    <div class="legend"><span><i class="sw" style="background:var(--green)"></i>rooted entry</span><span><i class="sw" style="background:var(--base)"></i>not rooted</span><span><i class="sw" style="background:none;border-top:2px dashed var(--ink2);height:0;width:18px"></i>mean share of non-rooted entries</span></div>
    <p class="takeaway" id="concept-take" aria-live="polite"></p>
  </div>

  <h3 id="h-browser">Every entry: input, prediction and outcome side by side</h3>
  <div class="card">
    <p class="q"><strong>What does the host share add for one entry?</strong> Pick any recorded entry. The panel sets its inputs beside two out-of-sample predictions of newcomer papers: a controls-only model (the baseline) and the same model with host share and co-transfer added (the method), then the count that happened.</p>
    <div class="controls">
      <label for="br-fold">Population</label>
      <select id="br-fold"><option value="screen">Screen (1,740)</option><option value="heldout">Held-out (1,097)</option><option value="mesh">MeSH (2,249)</option></select>
      <label for="br-q">Search</label>
      <input type="search" id="br-q" placeholder="concept or host subfield" autocomplete="off">
      <label for="br-filter">Show</label>
      <select id="br-filter"><option value="all">all entries</option><option value="rooted">rooted entries</option><option value="zero">entries with no newcomers</option><option value="hi0">high share, no newcomers</option></select>
      <label for="br-sort">Sort by</label>
      <select id="br-sort"><option value="A">host share, high first</option><option value="Y">newcomer papers, most first</option><option value="gain">method closer than baseline</option><option value="loss">method further than baseline</option></select>
    </div>
    <p class="status" id="br-status" aria-live="polite"></p>
    <div class="browser">
      <div>
        <div class="tablewrap"><table id="br-table"><caption class="sr">Host-entry events</caption><thead><tr><th scope="col">Concept</th><th scope="col">Host subfield, year</th><th scope="col" class="num">Host share</th><th scope="col" class="num">Newcomer papers</th></tr></thead><tbody></tbody></table></div>
        <div style="margin-top:8px"><button type="button" class="plain" id="br-more">Show 40 more</button></div>
      </div>
      <div class="detail card" id="br-detail" aria-live="polite"></div>
    </div>
    <p class="takeaway" id="br-take" aria-live="polite"></p>
  </div>

  <h3 id="h-margins">Does host share start uptake, or grow it?</h3>
  <div class="card">
    <p class="q"><strong>Which margin carries the effect?</strong> Each bar is a linear-probability estimate: percentage points added, per SD of host share, to the chance that an entry reaches the stated number of newcomer papers (<button class="term" data-term="extensive">extensive margin</button>). Thresholds rise from left to right.</p>
    <div class="controls">
      <div class="seg" role="radiogroup" aria-label="Population for the margin ladder" id="mg-fold">
        <label><input type="radio" name="mg" value="SCREEN" checked>Screen</label>
        <label><input type="radio" name="mg" value="HELDOUT">Held-out</label>
        <label><input type="radio" name="mg" value="MESH">MeSH</label>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="chart" id="mg-chart"></div>
    <div class="legend"><span><i class="sw" style="background:var(--accent)"></i>CI excludes 0</span><span><i class="sw" style="background:var(--base)"></i>CI includes 0</span><span>whiskers: 95% CI</span></div>
    <p class="small" id="mg-note"></p>
    <p class="takeaway" id="mg-take" aria-live="polite"></p>
  </div>
</div>
</section>

<!-- ============================================================ TRY IT -->
<section class="block" id="tryit" aria-labelledby="h-try">
<div class="wrap">
  <h2 id="h-try">Try it: move the cut-offs yourself</h2>
  <div class="card">
    <p class="q prose"><strong>What if we simply split entries at a host-share cut-off?</strong> Drag the sliders. The page recomputes, from the recorded entries, the share that reached at least <em>k</em> newcomer papers above and below the cut-off. These are raw shares with no fixed effects, so they mix concept, year and host differences that the paper's models remove; use them to see the pattern, not to replace the estimate.</p>
    <div class="controls">
      <label for="try-fold">Population</label>
      <select id="try-fold"><option value="screen">Screen</option><option value="heldout">Held-out</option><option value="mesh">MeSH</option></select>
      <label for="try-cut">Host-share cut-off (percentile)</label>
      <input type="range" id="try-cut" min="10" max="95" step="5" value="80" aria-describedby="try-cut-val">
      <output id="try-cut-val" for="try-cut" class="count"></output>
      <label for="try-k">At least <em>k</em> newcomer papers</label>
      <input type="range" id="try-k" min="1" max="10" step="1" value="1" aria-describedby="try-k-val">
      <output id="try-k-val" for="try-k" class="count"></output>
    </div>
    <div class="chart" id="try-chart"></div>
    <div class="legend"><span><i class="sw" style="background:var(--base)"></i>below cut-off</span><span><i class="sw" style="background:var(--accent)"></i>at or above cut-off</span><span><i class="sw" style="background:none;border-top:2px dashed var(--ink2);height:0;width:18px"></i>all entries</span></div>
    <p class="takeaway" id="try-take" aria-live="polite"></p>
  </div>
</div>
</section>

<!-- ============================================================ FAILS -->
<section class="block" id="fails" aria-labelledby="h-fails">
<div class="wrap">
  <h2 id="h-fails">Where it fails</h2>
  <div class="two">
    <div class="card">
      <p class="q"><strong>Which entries break the pattern?</strong> The effect is a gradient in expected counts, not a rule. Pick a failure type and a population.</p>
      <div class="controls">
        <div class="seg" role="group" aria-label="Failure type" id="fail-type">
          <button type="button" aria-pressed="true" data-f="hi0">High share, no newcomers</button>
          <button type="button" aria-pressed="false" data-f="lo1">Low share, rooted</button>
        </div>
        <label for="fail-fold">Population</label>
        <select id="fail-fold"><option value="screen">Screen</option><option value="heldout">Held-out</option><option value="mesh">MeSH</option></select>
      </div>
      <p class="status" id="fail-status" aria-live="polite"></p>
      <div class="faillist" id="fail-list"></div>
      <p class="takeaway" id="fail-take" aria-live="polite"></p>
    </div>
    <div class="card">
      <p class="q"><strong>Did network openness before take-off hold up?</strong> The paper's second question (RQ1): <button class="term" data-term="smd">standardised differences</button> in closure between concepts that later show <button class="term" data-term="sustained">sustained uptake</button> and matched controls. Only one measure survives <button class="term" data-term="holm">Holm correction</button> on the Held-out fold.</p>
      <div class="controls">
        <div class="seg" role="radiogroup" aria-label="Fold for closure estimates" id="cl-fold">
          <label><input type="radio" name="cl" value="heldout" checked>Held-out</label>
          <label><input type="radio" name="cl" value="screen">Screen</label>
        </div>
      </div>
      <div class="chart" id="cl-chart"></div>
      <div class="legend"><span><i class="sw" style="background:var(--accent)"></i>confirmed after Holm</span><span><i class="sw" style="background:var(--base)"></i>not confirmed</span><span><i class="sw" style="background:var(--orange)"></i>positive sign (not brokerage)</span></div>
      <p class="takeaway" id="cl-take" aria-live="polite"></p>
    </div>
  </div>
  <h3>What the paper does not show</h3>
  <ul class="plainlist prose">
    <li><strong>The main-arm folds are not true held-out tests.</strong> Event counts, population sizes and gating decisions were computed on both Screen and Held-out folds before outcomes were read. The independent evidence is the MeSH replication.</li>
    <li><strong>The stricter specification is underpowered.</strong> With concept-by-year and host-by-year fixed effects the Held-out fold keeps 250 of 972 events in 30 clusters and gives IRR 0.98 (95% CI 0.70 to 1.37). Switch the headline chart to “Primary FE” to see it.</li>
    <li><strong>The population is narrow.</strong> The pool is dominated by physics and computer-science concepts from arXiv, and MeSH covers only biomedicine-to-biomedicine entries. Social sciences, humanities and engineering are untested.</li>
    <li><strong>Binary rooting is null on the Held-out fold</strong> (<em>p</em> = 0.16). The effect is graded, not a threshold; the margin ladder above shows it fade at higher thresholds there.</li>
    <li><strong>Most entries are single papers.</strong> 87% of co-primary Screen events involve one entry-year paper. The pooled multi-team effect is positive (IRR 1.28, 95% CI 1.11 to 1.48), but the Held-out fold alone is underpowered for it.</li>
    <li><strong>Cluster-robust p-values run hot.</strong> The estimator rejects 10% to 11% of null shuffles (target 5%). Wild-cluster bootstrap and permutation tests agree with the headline (Held-out wild <em>p</em> = 0.012, permutation <em>p</em> = 0.026).</li>
    <li><strong>Host-specificity rests on a near-duplicate measure.</strong> The Balassa-index lift correlates 0.997 with the log of the continuous share within fixed effects, so it confirms the share rather than adding independent evidence.</li>
    <li><strong>The adopter-level result is Screen-only.</strong> Adopters are enriched for prior exposure to the entry partners (OR 3.09, 95% CI 2.32 to 4.28), most of all to origin-vocabulary partners (FOREIGN OR 2.88, ADJACENT 1.91, NATIVE 1.47). The design cannot separate absorptive capacity from topical proximity.</li>
  </ul>
</div>
</section>
</main>
